title: Twelve small books
hook: twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll

segments.voice: Yesterday, a river ran out from under the Temple door in Ezekiel's vision, rising as it went, until the salt sea was healed. Your line was everything lives where it flows. What did you let grow a little deeper? Today, Ezekiel's book closes, and a crowded scroll opens. Day eight hundred seventeen.

How do you keep a small book from getting lost? Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel each fill a long book of their own. After them come twelve more prophets, and some of their books are short enough to read on a bus ride. A herdsman from Tekoa. A man who ran from God by ship. A prophet who spoke against one neighboring nation, Edom. Instead of twelve little scrolls, tradition wrote them end to end, on one. Today's word is that scroll's name.
screen: `ONE SCROLL, TWELVE NAMES.` → `SHORT ENOUGH FOR A BUS RIDE.` → `WRITTEN END TO END.`

segments.voice: Trei Asar. It's Aramaic, and it simply means twelve. Not the twelve prophets, not the minor ones. Just: the Twelve. Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Say the names out loud once and they start to sound like a class roll call. Now, why one scroll? The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, asks a question about the order of the prophets. Near the start of Hosea's book come the words, the beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea, and the rabbis take that to mean his prophecy came early. So why isn't his book placed before Isaiah? Their answer is plain. Hosea is written together with the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. And because his book is small, it might get lost. A short scroll can slip behind a shelf. Twelve short books, sewn into one, stay found. So the scroll is a kind of protection for the quiet ones. And quiet is only on the outside. Inside these pages: a prophet whose broken marriage becomes a picture of God and Israel. A prophet who asks for justice to well up as waters. A runaway swallowed by a great fish. Lines still read aloud in synagogue. In the Talmud's list of the prophets, the Twelve appear under that one name, as a single book. Which is a fair picture of how a small voice can last: not alone, but bound in with others. Small books, big voices. Over the next stretch of days, this path walks through the scroll, one prophet at a time.
screen: `TREI ASAR: ARAMAIC FOR TWELVE.` · `HOSEA, JOEL, AMOS… MALACHI.` · then, large: `BECAUSE IT IS SMALL, IT MIGHT GET LOST.` · then: `BOUND IN WITH OTHERS, THEY LAST.`

segments.voice: The practice today is to read one short chapter. If there's a Bible or a reading app nearby, open to any of the Twelve, pick one short chapter, and read it slowly, start to finish, in the time the bell holds. No study notes. Just the words. If you'd rather not read right now, sit with the twelve names instead. Say them once, slowly, and let one of them stay. If you pray, you can ask to hear one small voice clearly today. The bell holds the time.
Trei Asar. Aramaic for twelve: the twelve short prophets, written together on one scroll so none of them would be lost. Today's word.
Your line: small books, big voices. Today, listen for one quiet person in a loud room, and give their words a second hearing. Day eight hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: In Jewish Bibles the twelve short prophets, Hosea through Malachi, are grouped as one book called Trei Asar, and passages from them are read as haftarot in synagogue.
